connector: Harriet ran from Miss Sarah’s whip and hid. Now she is home in her family’s cabin, and everyone knows the trouble is not over. In this chapter her mother and her father each try to help her, in different ways. Watch what Harriet refuses to do, even when doing it would make her life easier.

a.raw: miss sarah whipped the small slave girl but the brave child refused to cry out
a.fixed: Miss Sarah whipped the small slave girl, but the brave child refused to cry out.
a.why: Capital M on Miss (a title used with a name); capital S on Sarah; a comma before but joins two complete thoughts; the adjectives small and brave describe the nouns girl and child.

b.raw: old rit begged her stubborn daughter to smile but the proud girl would not do it
b.fixed: Old Rit begged her stubborn daughter to smile, but the proud girl would not do it.
b.why: Capitals on Old Rit, because it is her name; a comma before but joins two complete thoughts; the adjectives stubborn and proud describe the nouns daughter and girl.

scholar.journal-q1: … and explain what Harriet means when she says she feels hard inside.
scholar.journal-q2: … and explain why her parents don’t agree about smiling.
scholar.journal-q3: … and add a fourth note that says why one of your facts matters.

fill1.h1: Breathing out pushes air from inside you to outside. Which part means out?
fill1.why: ex- means out: ex + hale = to breathe out.

fill2.h1: The goods leave the country and go out to another one. Which part means out?
fill2.why: ex- means out: ex + port = to carry out.

fill3.h1: These games come once the regular season is over. Which part means after?
fill3.why: post- means after: post + season = the games after the season.

fill4.h1: A P.S. comes once the letter is already finished. Which part means after?
fill4.why: post- means after: post + script = written after.

notes.wgrd: Sort a biography’s facts into short notes: who, what happened, where, and why it matters. Read the notes back. What they all point to is the central idea.
vocab: A large farm where one crop is grown (in the South, often using slave labor).
A true book about someone’s life, written by another person.
To stretch out or reach further.
To put off until a later time.
notes.wordParts: ex- means “out of” or “former,” and post- means “after”: exit, extend, postpone, postscript.
notes.grammar: An adjective describes a noun. It tells what kind, how many, or which one, and it usually sits right before the noun: a cold spring, three geese.
notes.spelling: To split a long name, find the vowels, split between the consonants, and read each chunk. Names follow the same rules as any other word: Bal·ti·more.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. At the end of Chapter 1, Harriet was in a peck of trouble, and Chapter 2 is named for it. Today you’ll warm up, work with words, read Chapter 2, and study one sentence the way a writer does. Today’s question: what kind of trouble is Harriet in, and what does it tell us about her?
transcripts.wgrd: Today, read with four columns in your notebook: who, what happened, where, and why it matters. Keep each box short, three or four words. You’re collecting facts, not copying sentences. When the chapter ends, read your notes back. Whatever they all point at, that’s the central idea.
transcripts.dol: The model names a person with a title in front of her name. Titles and names both get capitals. The sentence to fix has two complete thoughts joined by a little word in the middle. Find that joining word, and decide what the sentence needs just before it. Then check the name.
transcripts.guide1: More practice with the two word parts that point out and point later. Today the words come from breathing, from trade, from sports, and from letters. That’s the point. These little parts travel everywhere. Once you know them, you can read words nobody has taught you yet.
transcripts.morphology: Every word today is missing its front. Don’t guess from the sound. Read the meaning on the right first, and ask one question: is this word about going out, or about coming after? The meaning will tell you which part belongs.
transcripts.vocabulary: These are the same four words as last time, and that’s on purpose. A word you meet once slips away. A word you meet four times starts to belong to you. This time, try the three steps without peeking. Say your guess out loud before you flip the card.
transcripts.grammar: Now you’re hunting two things at once: the describing words, and the nouns they describe. Every describing word is leaning on a noun. Find the pairs. If you can’t tell which is which, try a test. Take the word away, and see whether the sentence still names a thing.
transcripts.spelling: Some of these names have been chopped in the wrong places. Say each one slowly, beat by beat, the way you really say it. Where do the breaks in your voice fall? If the dots don’t match your breaks, that word is split wrong.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Freedom Watch is about small rebellions. Harriet can’t escape, and she can’t fight back. But there’s one thing she won’t do, no matter who asks her. Watch for it. Then ask yourself whether saying no quietly is still a kind of freedom, and what it costs her.
transcripts.read: Chapter 2 begins in the dark cabin where Harriet’s family lives. Pay attention to the cabin itself: the fireplace, the beds, and one thing her mother made by hand. Then listen to what her mother and her father each say about smiling. They don’t agree. Watch where Harriet stands.
transcripts.rwm: This sentence doesn’t say how Harriet feels. It gives her something to hold instead. Writers do this all the time. They hand the reader an object, and the feeling comes along with it. Ask why Sterling chose this object, out of everything in the cabin.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The questions ask why Miss Sarah is so angry, what each of Harriet’s parents does for her, and for three short fact notes. Keep those notes tight, like the columns you kept while you read. Then you’ll brainstorm questions for your own research about Harriet’s world.
transcripts.chapter: The third question asks for three fact notes. A good note is short and specific: a name, an action, a place. Not a feeling, and not a summary. Look back at your four columns. Choose the three facts someone would need to understand this chapter, and nothing extra.
transcripts.workshop: Research starts with curiosity. Today you don’t need answers yet, only questions, as many as you can think of. But notice the difference between a question you could decide and a question you could find out. The ones you can look up are the ones that make good research.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: going out, or coming after?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, saves scraps of cloth from the Big House and sews them, late at night by the fire, into a patchwork quilt of green and brown and yellow. It is the family’s only treasure. ex- means out, and post- means after. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. ex- = out, post- = after.
